lignes.texte: Everything we know about the birth of Western civilization is a lie.
The Ancient Greeks built modern society on nothing but logic and
reason. But the truth is much darker. Athens’ greatest minds were actually
powered by a state-sponsored, elite-enforced psychedelic ritual. It wasn’t accidental foraging.
It was a highly sophisticated chemical that was designed to suppress the masses.
And it’s been hiding in plain sight for 2,000 years.
The ruling elites of Athens guarded the secretive nature of the ritual with an iron fist. Revealing
any details was punishable by death. To even get a taste of it, some of the greatest minds
in history had to endure a gruelling, physical gauntlet known as the mysteries.
It all took place in a city 13 miles (21 km) northwest of Athens called Eleusis. There were
two general requirements to even take part in for the mysteries: participants couldn’t
have any blood on their hands - so murderers were out - and they had to speak and understand Greek.
Then the true ordeal began. The participants were forced to
trek through “The Sacred Way”, a path that honored the story of Demeter and
Persephone. It wasn’t a coincidence. The myth of Persephone focused on death and rebirth,
slipping between the underworld and life on earth. This procession was followed by bathing and animal
sacrifices. Then, they undertook a 9 day fast. Once they were weak, broken and pushed to the
brink, the participants were allowed to break their fast. They were handed a cup containing
a secretive brew. Kykeon.
To everyday Atheneans, it wasn’t anything special. It was a regular peasant drink made from barley,
water and mint. It was handed out to infantrymen every day.
But the kykeon handed out in Eleusis was different.
It was spiked with another special ingredient. One that was closely guarded by the priestesses
Today, scholars think that barley was hiding a little surprise:
a parasitic fungus known as ergot. Nature’s starting point for LSD.
Because of the strict rules surrounding the mysteries, no one really knows what took place.
Participants were sworn to secrecy.Because the priestesses would not let the secret out. However,
thanks to research by scientists Gordon Wasson and Albert Hofmann, we know what
the ergot fungus does to the human brain. Hofmann was working with the ergot alkaloids
when he accidentally created the LSD. Which means some of the best ancient philosophers,
playwrights, and military strategists in history were dosing it as well. Or
at least an ancient variation of it. So what happened when they took it?
Greeks and Romans like Plato, Cicero, and Marcus Aurelius had profound,
life-changing experiences during the mysteries, thanks in part to kykeon. A few details of the
mysteries did leak over time. Participants talked about seeing a transcendent preview of death,
and then were said to leave the experience with a new fearlessness about death itself.
But skeptics completely dismiss this theory. Ergot in its rawest form is a deadly toxin.
Without modern lab equipment, the philosophers of the Eleusinian
Mysteries wouldn’t just have a life-altering revelation. They’d suffer an agonizing death.
But scientists went a step further. Running tests, they found that using simple ancient techniques,
like treating ergot with water and wood ashes - or lye - removed its potential danger.
But it still kept the hallucinogenic and mind-altering properties intact.
So were history’s greatest thinkers tripping? New evidence suggests that’s the case.
A temple dedicated to two Eleusinian goddesses was discovered near Girona,
Spain. The excavation discovered a vase at the temple with the remnants of ergot in it. But they
also found the skeleton of a 25-year-old man that showed he had consumed ergot.
It’s just one of many indications that ancient people were not primitive when
it came to herbs and substances. They were more like master chemists who engineered sophisticated
pharmaceutical-grade biological tools to gatekeep power, war, and divine revelation.
Ancient Greece isn’t the only example. One cross-cultural survey found that,
among 488 societies in the old world, around 90% of these groups had some institutionalized
forms of altered states of consciousness. The academics studying the topic found
that “the ubiquity of mind-altering agents in traditional societies cannot be doubted - just
as the moods of industrial societies are set by a balance of caffeine, nicotine and alcohol”.
But there’s a massive difference between then and now.
Almost anyone today can get a beer or a cup of coffee. But societies gatekept
these substances for an elite few, depending on what the ruling classes needed from them.
Like the Vikings. Viking warriors were feared around the old world
for the devastation, looting, and violence they left in their wake. But there was a particular
type of Viking feared much more than the others: The Norse “berserker”.
Accounts of them are found all throughout the Viking Saga period,
roughly between 870 and 1030 AD. Icelandic poet Snorri Sturluson called them “mad as dogs
or wolves” and “strong as bears or wild oxen”. They seemed to be superhuman. They would enter
battle in a state that was often described as trance-like. Charging in with a blind rage,
the Berserkers would howl like animals and biting their shields. They sometimes
attacked their fellow Vikings because they lost the ability to distinguish
between friends and enemies. Their strength was immense; no one could go up against them.
Even more terrifying, they seemed almost immune to injury and pain. It was reported they would barely
even bleed when injured with blades. One historical account could be an
exaggeration… but all of them? Ethnobotanist Karsten Fatur,
of the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia, suspected more was at play. Specifically, a drug.
A dangerous substance that drove men insane with rage; but one that Viking leaders could utilize
to their advantage. A dose given at just the right time to almost guarantee victory in battle.
Fatur believes it was Hyoscyamus niger. Otherwise known as henbane.
Apparently the onset of “berserkergana” began with “bodily chills, shivering, and teeth chattering,
followed by swelling and reddening of the face. Then the rage broke out… once it abated,
the berserker would experience… physical fatigue and emotional numbness for a few days.”
Reading through these strange symptoms, and the almost superhuman strength of the Viking warriors,
Fatur started narrowing down possible herbs and plants. Many scientists thought it might
be a type of mushroom causing these symptoms. But it didn’t explain everything. Especially
the lack of bleeding people saw when berserkers were hit.
Fatur’s research was helped by the fact that few plants and herbs grown
in Scandinavia today are actually native to the region. But he discovered one that was; a weed
that was found everywhere. The black henbane. It causes a huge array of symptoms in humans.
Like dulling pain. That would explain why the berserkers didn’t seem to register hits like
normal warriors. It also confuses the brain’s ability to recognize faces. Something that might
explain why the berserkers would sometimes attack their own men. Henbane also lowers blood pressure
which would point to the lack of bleeding. Of course, the main symptom was the reason
why leaders gave it to their men in the first place: rage.
As Fatur writes: “this anger effect can range from agitation to full-blown rage
and combativeness depending on the dosage and mental set.” The mental state of a group of
men about to raid and attack a village would only intensify the drug’s “rage” side effect.
Essentially, henbane created a “biological tank” in an otherwise low-tech period. A super
soldier with significantly reduced pain sensitivity and dissociation.
Not all drugs in the ancient world were associated with anger and violence though. Some were actually
taken for their healing properties. And some were taken to make the users happy…and achieve
a feeling of true euphoria. Which is why Ancient Egypt
turned to the blue lotus flower. Though many alternative medicine
companies are marketing blue lotus today, they’re not actually selling the same thing Egyptians were
consuming. The actual flower is actually quite rare, and is considered endangered.
The blue lotus was incredibly important to Ancient Egypt.
It’s mentioned several times in the Book of the Dead. In 1922, archaeologist Howard Carter
found blue lotus petals covering the body of the recently unearthed Tutankhamun. It was
found on countless ancient papyri scrolls. It was such an integral party of Ancient
Egyptian culture, the blue lotus came to symbolize life and immortality itself.
So what exactly does it do? That’s the strange thing about it.
Ancient Egyptians may have been more aware of all its uses and effects than we are today.
As one article puts it, “the blue lotus remains an enigma”.
But researchers have uncovered some of its uses. As far as they can tell,
the blue lotus functioned as some kind of combination of ecstasy and anti-anxiety
medication, depending on how it was used. Ancient Egyptians would either add it to
wine directly, or make an infused oil from it and add that to wine.
It was almost always consumed in combination with alcohol, giving an extra powerful high.
The flower’s active ingredients are apomorphine and nuciferine.
The latter acts like an antipsychotic drug, bringing the user calmness. Researchers still
don’t actually know exactly why that is. The effects of apomorphine are more well
understood. It works like a dopamine agonist, inducing a sense of euphoria in the user.
Scientists have also found it can help with issues as varied as Parkinson’s disease and erectile
dysfunction, as it helps with muscle control. And it doesn’t stop there.
Researchers believe the blue lotus flower can also treat anxiety, insomnia, and a whole host
of other diseases they haven’t discovered yet. But ancient Egyptians were using it more for
its mind-altering properties than anything else. Because the blue lotus is entheogenic;
the scientific way of saying it’s a hallucinogen. IFLScience states the flower was used for
“religious, medicinal, and possibly psychological purposes, including treatments for various
ailments and psychoactive effects”. Other scholars believe elite ancient
Egyptians were using the blue lotus flowers and wine to orchestrate hallucinogenic,
sex fueled rituals. The blue lotus sold online today doesn’t hold a candle to the ancient
Egyptian version. One academic compared a sample of the endangered species to those
sold on places like Etsy. They found that the ancient flower’s nuciferine levels were through
the roof compared to the modern version. Ancient people got much higher than the
modern population could ever have guessed. That’s probably most true for the Scythians.
Little is known about them compared to other civilizations. That’s despite the fact they
ruled huge parts of Eurasia for a thousand years. Most of their history is catalogued by the Greeks
and Persians, who lived in fear of them. For years, archaeologists knew that
cannabis was important to Scythians. They just didn’t know how much.
Archaeologists once found a container of cannabis in a Scythian princess’ grave. She was buried over
2,500 years ago, and the container was among a collection of things she needed in the afterlife.
Clearly, the Scythians thought cannabis was such an important personal belonging,
it was necessary even in death. The drug also showed up in Scythian religion.
Soothsayers entered a trance-like state in order to predict the future for the Scythian people.
Greek historian Herodotus spoke endlessly about the Scythians’ love of cannabis,
as well as their drug-fueled exploits. He described them using cannabis to weave their
clothes. But he also referred repeatedly to their drug use, saying they used a special plant to make
smoke “that no Grecian vapour-bath can surpass.” Archaeologists couldn’t figure out exactly what
this substance was. Until the recent discovery of a Scythian kurgan - a grave mound, one the only
things Scythians left behind - in southern Russia. They dug up countless golden artifacts. Some
of them had an unexpected black, sticky residue inside.
Criminologists tested the substance and found a powerful combination: opium and cannabis.
Archaeologists Anton Gass and Andrei Belinski believe the ancient Scythians brewed and
drank the opium, while the cannabis burned nearby. Or as Gass puts it, “that both drugs
were being used simultaneously is beyond doubt.” Another reason many ancient people may have gotten
high is to dull the pain and symptoms of the diseases that the medicine of the time couldn’t
cure. That’s why the doctors and priests of the time created high-grade chemical compounds: to
help ancient people get high instead of suffering. One study by Greek professors found that doctors
used some drugs’ hypnotic effects for surgical operations and cauterization. Others used drugs
that affected the central nervous system for managing severe and chronic painful conditions.
These weren’t crude creations. Ancient people weren’t just picking herbs
from a field and chewing on them. They created scientific, exact processes, in which they would
produce drugs via “dehumidifaction/dessication, grinding, squeezing or boiling of the plants'
roots with a formation of a juice, oil or mush extract”. They would often add
wine to the plants’ opus to enhance the effect. So what was one of the first ever discovered uses
of drugs that are still around and used today? Cannabis was found in a 2,700 year old grave in
the Yanghai Tombs, China. Not just cannabis. Almost 2 pounds (789 grams) of weed. Found in
a single grave, that of an ancient shaman. There was so much, archaeologists initially
assumed it was coriander or something else that would be used for cooking or burning.
The most shocking part of the discovery came after the cannabis had been analyzed. While
cannabinoid plants had been found at other ancient sites, the concentration of tetrahydrocannabinol
in those finds - more commonly known as THC - was equal to the low THC concentration of such
plants that were growing wild at the time. The Yanghai Tombs discovery was different.
The cannabis archaeologists found here had a much higher THC concentration than wild plants
of the time. Though still not up to the high concentrations found today, it suggested that the
Gushi culture the tombs belonged to was actively cultivating cannabis in order to get high.
Back then, it would not have been ingested the same way it was today. Instead of being smoked,
it would have been burned alongside incense in a small, closed space. People who wanted
to get high would gather and inhale the vapors. Why does that matter so much? Because we may be
looking at the first use of weed by ancient people to get high; but also because, while the area is
remote today, it used to be around the Silk Road. One of the biggest and most important
trade routes in the ancient world. This find not only marks the start of
people purposely high, but the spread of it as well. As archaeobotanist Robert Spengler says,
“...that knowledge of cannabis smoking and specific… varieties of the cannabis
plant were among the cultural traditions that spread along these exchange routes.”
It seems like scientists have discovered the first instance of drug cultivation for a substance that
survives and thrives today. The modern world didn’t just
inherit history… it’s still smoking it. When people want to relax they turn to
their drug of choice. But how bad is smoking or drinking really? Watch Alcohol vs Weed - Which
is Actually Worse For You? To find out what’s going on inside your body. Or click on this.
